Modern knowledge graphs are largely built through automated information extraction from text using named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction, and coreference resolution. Systems like OpenIE extract subject-predicate-object triples from unstructured text at scale. [0] Large language models have proven effective at extracting structured entity and relationship information from text. Given a passage, an LLM can identify entity names, types, and the relationships between them in a single forward pass, often outperforming traditional pipeline-based extraction on complex, implicit relationships. [1] Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph from the document corpus by extracting entities and relationships using an LLM. At query time, it traverses the graph structure to find relevant connected information, enabling multi-hop reasoning that flat vector search cannot support. Microsoft's GraphRAG system is a prominent example, using hierarchical community detection and community report generation to support both local and global queries. [2] An ontology defines the types of entities and relationships that can exist in a knowledge graph and the logical constraints on how they relate. Widely-used ontologies include Schema.org (used for web markup), DBpedia (extracted from Wikipedia infoboxes), and domain-specific ontologies in healthcare (SNOMED CT), biology (Gene Ontology), and finance. [3] Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relationships as dense vectors in a continuous space, enabling downstream machine learning tasks. TransE, one of the earliest and most influential models, represents relationships as translations in embedding space: if (head, relation, tail) is a valid triple, then the head vector plus the relation vector should approximately equal the tail vector. Later models include RotatE (relations as rotations in complex space), DistMult (bilinear scoring), and ComplEx (complex-valued embeddings). [4] A knowledge graph is a structured representation of facts about entities and the relationships between them. It organizes information as a graph where nodes represent entities (people, places, organizations, concepts) and edges represent typed relationships between those entities. Each edge carries a specific relationship type, such as "founded_by," "located_in," or "works_at." [5]

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances large language model outputs by grounding them in relevant external documents retrieved at query time. [0] RAG was introduced by Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research in the 2020 paper "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks." [1] RAG combines a parametric memory component (the LLM's trained weights) with a non-parametric memory component (a searchable document corpus). [2] RAG systems also support citations — since the answer is grounded in specific retrieved passages, the system can point to exact source documents, improving interpretability and trustworthiness. [3] RAG addresses issues with large language models, such as knowledge being hallucinated or misremembered, by keeping knowledge external and retrievable. [4] RAG systems also support hybrid search, combining both vector and keyword search to outperform either approach alone on mixed query types. [5]
HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) generates a hypothetical answer to the query first, then uses that as the retrieval query, often improving recall. [0]

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is an approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm that builds a multi-layer graph where each layer is a navigable small-world network. Queries start at the top layer and greedily descend to the bottom layer, following edges to progressively closer nodes. HNSW achieves sub-millisecond query times on million-scale datasets. [0]
